1.pericope_label: Now concerning the collection for the saints

schools.summary: Chrysostom asks why almsgiving is the one point of practical morality Paul treats at the close, when elsewhere he ends with temperance, meekness and long-suffering together. His answer is that the greater part of the letter had already been ethical — the fornicator chastised, those going to law before Gentiles corrected, drunkards and gluttons terrified, the seditious condemned, unworthy communicants sentenced, love expounded — so that only the pressing matter of aid for the saints remained.

Gill identifies the saints as the poor believers at Jerusalem, impoverished either by the spoiling of their goods under persecution or by the selling of their possessions into a common stock since exhausted, partly by living on it and partly by spending it to spread the gospel among the Gentiles. Calvin traces the occasion to the famine Agabus foretold and grounds the duty in gratitude, the Gentile churches being bound, on pain of great ingratitude, to relieve the place from which they had received the gospel.

Henry watches the tact of the appeal: no peculiar service is demanded, only the rule already given to Galatia, and Paul names those churches to stir emulation, since a congregation excelling most others in gifts and probably in wealth would not suffer itself to come behind any in bounty.
Wesley spares the verse one line and it is the sharpest in the chapter: the saints is a more solemn and a more affecting word than if he had said the poor.

Ellicott makes Paul's choice of the word saints the true ground of the claim, and reads the need itself as evidence that the Jerusalem community of goods had failed, Christianity being largely recruited from the lower classes. Barnes hears the definite article as proof the matter was already familiar, so that every instruction concerns the manner and not the duty, and insists the word rendered order does not mean Paul assumed authority to tax them. On the noun for collection Barnes reports that it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament nor in the classical writers; Robertson corrects him from the papyri and inscriptions, where it is chiefly found of religious collections for a god or a temple.

2.pericope_label: Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store

schools.summary: Gill guards against over-reading the plural: an ancient copy of Beza's adds the Lord's day and the Syriac and Arabic render every first day, but the apostle intends some one first day, not a standing weekly ordinance, since his stated reason is that there be no gatherings when he comes. Calvin twice declines Chrysostom's readings, thinks the apostles at first retained the day already in use and only later, pressed by superstition, set it aside for the resurrection day, and reads Paul's warning elsewhere against distinguishing days as aimed at religion rather than external order.

Clarke draws the firmest conclusion, reading the verse as a strong argument for keeping the Christian sabbath, and finds the practice's shape in the synagogue, where the Jews collected for the poor on the sabbath and kept a purse of alms. Wesley presses the measure: not the rich only, but let him that hath little gladly give of that little; a tenth is merely the lowest rule of Christian prudence, and the more excellent way is to stint yourself to no proportion at all but lend to God all you can.

Barnes notes the Jews used sabbath for the week itself, so the first day is meant, and Robertson adds that the cardinal stands for the ordinal after the Hebrew fashion of the Greek Old Testament. Ellicott observes the resurrection day had already become the day for Christian worship though not yet by the later title. On where the money rested the three divide: Robertson takes the phrase plainly as by himself, in his home, and Barnes stresses the privacy of setting a portion apart calmly and on principle rather than under pathetic appeals, while Ellicott rejects the domestic reading outright, since the stated object is a sum ready in bulk on the apostle's arrival.

3.pericope_label: Whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters, them will I send

schools.summary: Barnes lays out the punctuation dispute: Macknight and Doddridge take the letters to be sent by the Corinthian church certifying its messengers, the reading the usual pointing supports, while Griesbach, Locke, Rosenmuller, Bloomfield, Beza, Hammond, Grotius and Whitby put the comma after approve so that Paul supplies the letters. Mill doubted the Greek allowed it; Barnes thinks the weight of names settles it. Ellicott reads a man still deciding, governed by how much was collected, and adds that Paul valued his apostolic dignity enough to feel it beneath the office, though not beneath himself, to carry a very small sum. Robertson notes the letters made the appointment formal, and that no Corinthian name appears in Luke's list of companions.

Clarke asks why Paul should want letters of approbation for men he would shortly meet face to face, and suggests either that the reference is to letters the Corinthians had already sent him or that Bishop Pearce is right to render it ye shall have approved, in which case the difficulty vanishes; the alternative punctuation, he says, seems most natural.

Calvin states the principle the arrangement serves: we give cheerfully when we know for certain that what we give is well laid out, so the apostle points them to a method of assurance in the selecting of approved persons, and his offer of his own services shows he has the matter at heart. Gill glosses the opening clause simply, that the coming meant is to Corinth, and very quickly.

4.pericope_label: And if it be meet that I go also, they shall go with me

schools.summary: Gill reads the condition as bearing on the size of the gift rather than the convenience of the apostle, noting that the Syriac renders it if this work should be worthy that I should go and the Arabic if the thing should be worthy to go with me; by which, he observes drily, Paul is artfully pressing them toward a good collection.

Robertson confirms that sense from the grammar, rendering it if the collection be worthy of the going as to me also, and remarks that once the construction is seen the awkward phrase clears up. Barnes puts it practically, that Paul would go if his presence would further the object, satisfy the Corinthians better, or be needed to guide the men they sent, and commends Paley's account of the apostle's handling of money as management so delicate as never to excite suspicion.

Clarke quotes Paley at length. Paul disclaims inspired authority for these directions, speaking not by commandment but on occasion of the forwardness of others — and who with a sinister purpose would thus lower the credit of his own recommendation? He asserts the general right of ministers to maintenance yet refuses it himself, holding it better to die than that any man should make his professions of disinterestedness void. And he repeatedly proposes associates in the management of the bounty, pointedly not colleagues of his own appointment but men elected by the contributors. Wesley compresses the whole safeguard into five words: to remove any possible suspicion.

5.pericope_label: Now I will come unto you, when I shall pass through Macedonia

schools.summary: Gill hears the promise as a rebuttal, since some had given out that Paul would never come to them again and hoped they should never see him. Calvin sets out the common opinion that the letter came from Philippi before rejecting it for Ephesus on three grounds — that Paul says he will remain where he is until Pentecost, that he greets them from the churches of Asia rather than of Macedonia, and that he states in the second epistle that he crossed into Macedonia only after this letter had gone. Calvin adds that a straight course to Achaia was open to him and that the Macedonian circuit was long and disagreeable, so that choosing it shows his affection.

Henry turns the travel plan into a rule: the heart of a truly Christian minister must be much toward the people among whom he has long laboured with remarkable success. Some at Corinth despised Paul and had made a faction against him, yet many loved him tenderly; and as for the rest, he might hope a longer stay would reduce them to a better temper and rectify what was out of order — a prospect Henry calls a just reason for an apostle to make his abode in a place.

Ellicott is blunt that the note at the end of the chapter placing the writing at Philippi rests on a misreading of this clause, since Paul states an intention for his journey and not his present whereabouts. Barnes explains that Paul had abandoned the order of the visit, not the visit itself, and Robertson identifies the present indicative as the futuristic use, meaning simply I plan to pass through.

Clarke explains why the route counts as a detour worth mentioning, Macedonia lying at the upper end of the Aegean and very far out of the direct line from Ephesus to Corinth, and reports that almost all now allow the letter came from Ephesus. Wesley's whole comment is that Paul purposes going that way.

6.pericope_label: That ye may bring me on my journey whithersoever I go

schools.summary: Gill accounts for the hedging, noting that Paul could not be certain what calls in Providence might arise elsewhere, so the winter is offered as a possibility and not a promise.

Clarke supplies the whole projected itinerary — Pentecost at Ephesus, then Macedonia and probably the summer there, then Corinth in the autumn and the winter with them — and reads the sending forward materially: in most cases the churches paid his expenses on to the next, and where a church did not, he worked at his trade to acquire the means of travelling.

Robertson notes that the phrase for it may be is a participle used as an adverb, found in Plato and Xenophon but nowhere else in the New Testament, and confirms from the record that Paul did stay three months and did have to flee a plot. Barnes glosses the sending forward as accompanying and furnishing him, observing that apostles customarily travelled attended by members of the churches. Ellicott refuses to stop at provision, holding that the phrase implies Paul should set out with the good wishes and blessing of his Corinthian friends; he also points out that where Paul would go from Corinth was settled for him in the event, a conspiracy discovered in time forcing the Syrian voyage to be abandoned for a route by Troas.

7.pericope_label: For I will not see you now by the way; but I trust to tarry a while with you

schools.summary: Gill catches the tone of the refusal: Paul will not merely look in on them and be gone, like a wayfaring man who turns aside for a single night.

Robertson confirms that the Greek phrase carries the casualness of our own idiom for something said in passing, and describes the closing condition as one of the third class, the form used for what is genuinely open, concluding in five words that Paul did everything in the Lord. Barnes reads the same reservation from Paul's temper rather than his syntax and reaches the same place: the apostle does not use the language of certainty and confidence, but felt his dependence upon God and regarded everything as under his direction, the same qualification appearing earlier in this letter. Ellicott records only that this is one more reference to the changed intention.

Clarke notes how easy the omitted visit would have been, from Ephesus to Corinth being merely a crossing of the Aegean and comparatively a short passage, so that what Paul refuses is a kind of visit and not a distance. Wesley reduces the clause to a schedule: not until I have been in Macedonia.

8.pericope_label: But I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost

schools.summary: Calvin argues from this clause that the letter came from Ephesus, since Paul speaks of where he is and not of a place reachable only by a long circuit, and then contests Erasmus, who rendered the word as a bare interval on what Calvin judges frivolous conjecture. Erasmus objected that no Christian Pentecost yet existed, which Calvin grants, and that the Jewish feast cannot be meant since Paul condemns the superstitious observance of days — which Calvin refuses, holding that Paul waited not from regard to the day but because a larger assembly would gather and an opportunity of propagating the gospel be presented; the definite article, he adds, will not let the word mean a mere count of fifty. Gill reaches the same conclusion independently: the feast was abrogated at the death of Christ and is named only to mark the length of the stay.

Barnes takes the naming of Ephesus as decisive for the letter's origin, noting that it is by incidental indications of just this kind that the epistles are placed at all. Robertson concludes Paul is writing in the spring before the feast and holds that the uproar raised by Demetrius apparently hurried him out of the city before his own date. Ellicott places it about Easter, and reads the plan as formed under pressure, the hostility of enemies increasing while a door had opened wide — duty to be done and danger to be faced being together sufficient indication to such a man of where he ought to be found.
Clarke thinks it very probable the stay ran its full course and that all these journeys were taken exactly as the apostle projected them, which sets him directly against Robertson.

9.pericope_label: For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries

schools.summary: Gill canvasses three accounts of the open door — the populousness of Ephesus, the conversion of certain great men there, or the desire that had appeared in many to hear — and judges the third, putting it as two doors at once, a door of utterance in the apostle and a door of entrance in them. Calvin says the metaphor is a common one, calls the door great because many might be gained and effectual because the Lord blessed the labour and by the Spirit rendered the doctrine powerful, and presses the adversaries hardest: Paul never chose a place for his own convenience but presented himself of his own accord where he must contend most keenly, knowing that the fiercer the assault the more resolute he had to be.

Clarke alone reaches for a particular allusion, suggesting the flinging open of the great doors of the Circus Maximus before the chariot races, in which case the adversaries are the competitors already in the field; he also reports Bishop Pearce reading the second adjective not as effectual but as full of labour, so that the door is one the apostle sees will require much toil. Wesley distributes the two words neatly, the door being great as to the number of hearers and effectual as to the effects wrought upon them, and adds that there must always be adversaries where Satan's kingdom shakes.

Robertson goes to the evidence for the disputed adjective, a late word found in the papyri of a medical preparation tolerably strong and, in its related form, of a mill in working order, of tilled land and of wrought iron; Paul means at least that he has a great opportunity for work. He describes the opponents as lined up against Paul, agrees they are named as a reason for staying, then admits the difficulty honestly — and yet Paul suddenly leaves, hinting at much we should like to know more of. Barnes observes that the opening of a great door is often the very occasion of increased opposition, and that Paul read it as evidence the Spirit was at work and his presence needed to strengthen young converts.

10.pericope_label: Now if Timotheus come, see that he may be with you without fear

schools.summary: Chrysostom turns the caution around and offers the most striking reading on the bench. Someone may think the advice unworthy of Timothy's courage, he says, but it is not said on Timothy's account at all — it is said for the hearers' sake, lest by their designs against him they injure themselves, since Timothy's station was always in the way of dangers. What Paul fears is that from boldness toward the disciple they will proceed to the teacher and grow worse, or exact from the messenger satisfaction for the master's rebuke; and Chrysostom hears the emphasis fall on the last words — tell me not of those without, the Gentiles and unbelievers; it is your part I require, you for whom the whole letter was composed.

Gill notes that Paul had already dispatched Timothy and could not say whether the roads would prevent him, from which it is plain the letter was not carried by him whatever the subscription claims. Calvin narrows the danger, denying that Timothy's life was at risk and locating the threat in the many enemies of Christ who would oppose him, then generalises: the church ought to be concerned for the preservation of its ministers' lives, and the more a man is endowed with gifts for edification and applies himself to it, the dearer his life should be to us.

Henry puts the risk bluntly: Timothy came not only to direct but to blame, censure and reprove the culpable, into a church wholly in factions where some were rich and many proud on account of wealth and spiritual gifts — and proud spirits cannot easily bear reproof. It was therefore reasonable to think young Timothy might be roughly used, and Henry draws the rule that Christians should bear faithful reproofs from their ministers rather than terrify and discourage them from their duty.

Ellicott explains how the messengers might be overtaken by the letter, since Timothy and Erastus were to delay at the Macedonian churches while this went by a more direct route, and presses the danger further: Timothy was young in years and young in the faith, probably of a constitutionally weak and timid nature, and officially very subordinate, in a church where some had questioned the apostle's own authority. Robertson agrees in a sentence that Paul evidently had reason to fear the treatment Timothy might receive.

Clarke calls the subscription very exceptionable, since Timothy had been sent with Erastus from Ephesus into Macedonia. Wesley takes the closing clause as the true ground of reverence to pastors and concludes that those who work the Lord's work no one ought to despise.

11.pericope_label: Let no man therefore despise him: but conduct him forth in peace

schools.summary: Barnes expects the contempt from the wealthy and proud who valued themselves on wisdom and experience, and holds that a young minister who conducts himself according to his calling should find his youth no barrier to the confidence even of aged Christians but rather a reason to treat him with affection. Ellicott sets the arrangement in sequence: Timothy and Erastus went before the letter, at a time when the full state of Corinth had not reached the apostle, and now Titus is sent with it — a man in energy and firmness a striking contrast to Timothy while equally sharing Paul's spirit. Robertson supplies the sober outcome, that Timothy did later return to Ephesus without much success.

Gill widens the word, holding that to neglect to take care of Timothy would itself be to despise him, since he was employed in the same honourable work as the apostle, and infers that ministers' lives ought to be defended and their persons treated with esteem. Calvin suspects this is exactly Paul's point, that failure to be concerned for Timothy's safety would already count as contempt, and adds a third sense, that they should not undervalue him out of ignorance of his worth; he glosses the phrase in peace as meaning in safety.

Clarke breaks from the others twice. Following Bishop Pearce he would repunctuate the clause so that it reads accompany him upon his journey, that he may come to me in peace, taking the word as safety; and he denies the usual sense of the last clause altogether, holding that it is the brethren already with Paul who are doing the looking, so that the meaning is I, with the brethren, am looking for him. Wesley reads it the other way in four words, taking the brethren to be those accompanying Timothy.

12.pericope_label: As touching our brother Apollos, I greatly desired him to come unto you

schools.summary: Gill explains why the verse is needed: Apollos was senior to Timothy, an eloquent preacher well known and greatly approved at Corinth, so the apostle takes trouble to show that sending the one and not the other was no fault of his. Calvin sets out the suspicion being headed off — the better they knew Apollos the readier they would be to conjecture that matters had been contrived out of some offence taken, and they might well ask why these men were sent rather than he.

Clarke states the reason plainly, that a faction had been set up in Apollos's name at Corinth and he probably thought it imprudent to go lest his presence give that party strength or countenance. Wesley suspects the same, that his coming might increase the divisions.

Barnes reasons that Apollos had perhaps left Corinth on account of the dissensions and would not return while they lasted, especially as the partisans had tried to make him the head of a party, and reports from the Latin fathers that he did return once the differences were settled. Robertson is bluntest — Apollos had left in disgust over the strife involving both him and Paul, and had had enough of partisan quarrelling over preachers. Ellicott draws out what the exchange shows of both men: Paul, free from the smallest spark of personal jealousy, had wished the very man whose name was a faction's banner to carry this letter, and that unselfishness is equalled by the thoughtful reluctance of Apollos; in the thought of these teachers, Ellicott adds, convenient meant the good of Christ's church and not the ease of any individual man.

13.pericope_label: Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong

schools.summary: Clarke makes the observation that governs the verse — the terms in it are all military — and reads it through as a field order: keep your scouts out and your sentinels at their posts; keep in your ranks and close together, for on your unity your preservation depends, and if the enemy divides one part of this sacred army from another your rout is inevitable; when attacked do not flinch, resist, press forward, strike home, keep compact, conquer; where one division is overmatched, strengthen it and hold the position, sustain each other and do not fear, for fear will enervate you — your cause is good, Christ is your Captain in the field, and should you even die in the contest the victory is yours. He also gives the watching five directions: against evil, for opportunities to receive and to do good, over each other in love, and that none draw you aside. Wesley reduces the four commands to a line apiece, closing with be strong to do and to suffer all his will.

Gill rules out a wrong object first, that they are not to watch for the coming of Apollos but over themselves and one another, and against sin in its first motions, against Satan whose wiles are many and cunning, and against the false teachers of whom that church had many. Calvin sees the same campaign: because the warfare is incessant the watch must be incessant too, and he defines watchfulness of spirit as meditating on the things of God while disentangled from earthly cares, since the cares and lusts of the world, with idleness and carelessness, are a kind of spiritual drunkenness that leaves the mind drowsy and stupid. As we are naturally weak, he adds, we must be told to gather strength and not assumed to have it.

Henry reads standing fast as a double command — to stand for the faith of the gospel and maintain it even to death, and to stand in it, abiding in its profession and yielding to its influence — and warns them not to surrender God's revelation for the world's wisdom. It is by faith alone that a man keeps his ground in an hour of temptation, and by it that we overcome the world both when it fawns and when it frowns, when it tempts and when it terrifies.

Barnes takes the first imperative to mean keep awake and suggests the figure is drawn from a sentinel set to guard a camp, lest an enemy come suddenly upon an army locked in sleep; he notes that the verb for playing the man appears nowhere else in the New Testament though it is frequent in the Greek Old Testament and common in the classical writers, meaning simply to show oneself a man and not a coward. Robertson confirms both verbs, the first meaning stay awake and the later one, in the middle voice, play the man.

14.pericope_label: Let all your things be done with charity

schools.summary: Barnes glosses the opening phrase as simply all that you do, and explains why the apostle risks a repetition: it is given again because of its great importance and because it sums up everything he has said in the letter, the long treatment of love and the ordering of the assembly both coming to rest here. Charity was to regulate all they did; it is a simple rule, and if it were observed everything would be done well.

Gill spreads the word all across three relations: their whole obedience to Christ should spring from and be done in love to him; their conduct toward one another should be governed by a charity which bears all things and covers a multitude of sins; and their church business should be handled not with strife and vainglory but in peace and mutual affection, with concern for the good of the whole body and the glory of God. Without that grace, he adds, it signifies little what men either have or do — and the exhortation was the more necessary to a church so full of factions and divisions. Calvin calls it the rule for all our dealings with one another and names the disease it answers: the Corinthians erred chiefly in this, that every one looked to himself without caring for others.

15.pericope_label: The house of Stephanas, the firstfruits of Achaia

schools.summary: Barnes warns that the entreaty does not complete itself until the next verse, so that what stands between is a parenthesis giving the reasons for the deference afterwards required, and fills in the shape the household's service took — aiding the ministry, showing hospitality, providing for the wants of others, helping the apostles on their journeys. Ellicott points to a play upon words in the Greek that can scarcely be rendered, they having ordered themselves to the ministry of the saints and the Corinthians being exhorted to order themselves under them in turn; he adds the delicate circumstance that these men, faithful amid the faithless, might be suspected of carrying tales, so that Paul commends them expressly as friends who came on behalf of the whole body. Robertson lands on the same verb and calls the statement remarkable and worthy of attention still — this noble family appointed themselves to be ministers to the saints who needed it, nobody having appointed them; personal work for Christ, he adds, is still the only way to win the world for Christ.

Calvin draws the boldest claim in the verse: we know from daily experience how much it matters that those whom God has adorned with the most distinguished gifts should hold the highest authority, so let honour be conferred upon the good, let their counsels carry the greatest weight, and let others allow themselves to be governed by their prudence — for God manifests himself in showing us the gifts of his Spirit, and unless we would appear to despise God we should yield willingly to those on whom he has conferred them. He is careful, though, not to let priority alone confer rank: it is where perseverance accompanies priority that honour is rightly given. Gill reads the whole account of Stephanas as an argument for the submission afterwards required.

Clarke gives the household a large place, calling them the chief instruments of supporting the work of God in Achaia, of which work they had themselves been the firstfruits. Wesley glosses the title flatly as the first converts in that province.

16.pericope_label: That ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us

schools.summary: Clarke states the narrow view flatly: the submission recommended does not imply obedience, but a kind and courteous demeanour, due regard for such men as special instruments in God's hand — and he cites Kypke as vindicating that sense from the word's use elsewhere of Christians yielding to one another and of the younger to the elder. Wesley catches the reciprocity in three words, that the Corinthians are to submit in their turn, so repaying the free service they had received, and extends the charge to everyone who labours in the gospel, with a fellow-labourer or without one.

Gill reaches considerably further, dividing the duty by the kind of service rendered: where men minister to poor saints it means assisting them and putting it in their power to discharge that work fully; where men labour in the word it means attending their ministrations, receiving the truths they deliver with faith and love, hearkening to their admonitions, regarding the censures and reproofs they pass by the authority of the church, and living in subjection to the laws of Christ's house. He qualifies it pointedly, however: the truths are to be received only so far as they appear agreeable to the word of God, which sets a limit inside the very duty he has drawn so widely.

Barnes takes the word to mean showing proper deference and regard, treating such people with distinguished respect for what they have done, and suggests that since Corinth was a thoroughfare the charge would cover others of Paul's friends passing through. Robertson says plainly that this completes the exhortation begun in the previous verse — the family of Stephanas took the lead in good works and the Corinthians are to follow such leaders — then turns it on his own readers: this is our great problem still, to find great leaders and many loyal followers.

17.pericope_label: I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus

schools.summary: Clarke identifies the errand at once: it was by these three that the Corinthians sent the letter which this epistle was largely written to answer, and he narrows what they supplied to two possibilities — additional communications beyond the letter, from which Paul had a fuller account of their spiritual state, or some contribution toward his support in his travels. Wesley quietly adopts the other side of the ambiguity, saying they performed the offices of love which the Corinthians could not perform by reason of their absence, and notes that by the time this was written the three had already gone home though the joy of their arrival remained in the apostle's heart.

Barnes explains that the noun rendered that which was lacking does not occur in the classical writers and means simply a want, which may be of support, sustenance, aid, consolation, information or counsel, so that what the Corinthians failed to furnish can only be conjectured; he offers three possibilities and supposes Stephanas was chosen for the errand as one of the oldest and most respected members. He notes the other two are named nowhere else in the New Testament, though he and Clarke both report that Fortunatus outlived Paul and later carried Clement's letter from Rome back to Corinth. Robertson refuses to choose at all, and for a reason of grammar rather than history: the phrase can mean either that these men filled up his lack of the Corinthians or their lack of him, either makes perfectly good sense, both were true, and which Paul meant we cannot tell. He pauses too on the word for their coming, the very term used of the coming of Christ.

Gill thinks they were very probably of the household of Chloe, and observes that whether they came of their own accord or as the church's messengers, one had been baptised by Paul and perhaps all were converted under his ministry.

18.pericope_label: For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them

schools.summary: Gill explains what the refreshment consisted in: the sight of the three gave joy, their discourse more, and most of all the account they brought — for though much in it was disagreeable and is the occasion of this letter, Paul's spirit had been depressed by reports from another quarter and by the fear that matters stood worse than they did, and from these brethren he learned that many in the church had great grace and large gifts, stood steadfast in the faith, opposed the false teachers vigorously, and sought in everything the welfare of the church.

Barnes lays four readings of the clause and yours side by side: Locke, that the visit removed the suspicions and fears standing on either side; Bloomfield, that by supplying the Corinthians' absence these men benefited both, Paul gaining information and they gaining his counsel; Doddridge, that as they had refreshed Paul by their obliging behaviour they had no doubt often refreshed the Corinthians by their ministrations at home. His own judgement gathers the rest, that the visit would benefit both sides with comfort and a good understanding and an increase of mutual attachment. On the charge that follows he takes acknowledge to mean receive them affectionately, recognise them as brethren, and regard with deference the counsel they might offer. Robertson notes that the verb for refreshing is the very one Jesus used of the rest he offers to those who come to him.

Clarke takes the simplest line on the disputed clause, that what contributed greatly to Paul's comfort must for that reason increase theirs, and Wesley says the same in five words, inasmuch as you share in my comfort. Clarke then turns the instruction into a general rule of the sharpest kind, one that answers the party spirit this whole letter has been fighting: let all be held in esteem in proportion to their work and usefulness, for when that is made the measure of respect, foolish and capricious attachments will have no place at all, and a man will be honoured in proportion to his merit.

19.pericope_label: The churches of Asia salute you, with the church that is in their house

schools.summary: Calvin calls the phrase a magnificent eulogium, since the name of the Church is here applied to a single family, and holds that all the families of the pious ought to be so ordered as to be so many little churches; he rejects the alternative word Erasmus preferred as foreign to Paul's design, since the apostle meant not to designate a crowd by a common term but to speak honourably of the management of a Christian household. Gill notes the Syriac makes it all the churches, and argues that from Philippi Paul would have greeted them from the churches of Macedonia rather than of Asia.

Henry takes the household reading and draws the consequence out: every Christian family should in some respects be a Christian church — cast away on a foreign shore with no other believers they should be a church themselves, if large enough, and use all the ordinances, while in ordinary cases they should live under Christian rules and daily offer up Christian worship, for wherever two or three are gathered and Christ is among them there is a church. He also pauses over the presence of greetings at all and makes it a point of principle: Christianity does by no means destroy civility and good manners, and those misrepresent religion who take any encouragement from it to be sour and morose; nor are such salutations empty compliments, for those who salute in the Lord wish their brethren all good from the Lord and breathe out their wishes in fervent prayer.

Clarke reads the phrase of the congregation rather than the family, pointing out that there were no churches or chapels built at that time so that assemblies were necessarily held in private houses, Aquila and Priscilla devoting theirs to the purpose as Philemon and Nymphas did after them; he makes the same argument as Gill against Philippi. Wesley records that the apostle's acquaintance with the couple began during their stay at Corinth.

Barnes explains that Asia is here narrowed to the country around Ephesus, of which that city was the centre and capital, and glosses the warmth of the greeting — much in the Lord means as Christians, wishing one another the blessing and favour of the Lord. Robertson remarks how rapidly the gospel had spread out from Ephesus, and adds the circumstance that makes Clarke's reading concrete: Paul had long since left the synagogue for the lecture hall of Tyrannus, but Aquila and Prisca opened their own house for the services, and the churches had to meet where they could. Ellicott offers a third and narrower possibility, that the phrase means a group of foreigners then resident in Ephesus who met there for worship, as distinct from those converted in the city.

20.pericope_label: Greet ye one another with an holy kiss

schools.summary: Cyril of Jerusalem states most fully what the kiss meant, describing the moment in the liturgy when the deacon cries aloud, receive ye one another, and let us kiss one another. Do not think, he warns, that this kiss is of the same character as those given in public by common friends; it is not such. This kiss blends souls one with another and courts entire forgiveness for them; it is the sign that our souls are mingled together and have banished all remembrance of wrongs. He grounds it in the Lord's command that a man who remembers at the altar that his brother has something against him should leave his gift, go and be reconciled first, and then come and offer — and so concludes that the kiss is reconciliation, and that this is why it is holy, citing both Paul's holy kiss here and Peter's kiss of charity.

Calvin thinks the reference is not to greeting in general but to a solemn kiss with which they saluted one another in the sacred assembly, and says he could easily believe that from apostolic times it was used in connection with the administration of the Supper — a conjecture Cyril's account independently confirms. His text carries a long note gathering the evidence: Justin Martyr describing how after the prayers the Christians embrace each other with a kiss, Tertullian treating it as an ordinary part of the Lord's day services, Origen deriving the custom from this very precept, and the Apostolical Constitutions prescribing that the men apart and the women apart salute each other in the Lord. The note is nevertheless cautious about pressing the precept, holding that Paul certainly meant them to salute one another on receiving the letter but that he meant to make it an everlasting ordinance has never been proved; and it adds that the very prevalence of the custom probably gave rise to the calumny that Christians indulged in licentiousness at their meetings. Gill offers three candidates for the brethren who send the greeting.

Clarke explains the background, that the ancient patriarchs and the Jews generally kissed one another whenever they met, this being with them a token of friendship and peace much as the shaking of hands is with us, and the primitive Christians naturally followed the example.

Ellicott says the kiss was the ordinary form of affectionate greeting in the East, taken over by the Church and called holy when it passed between those whose bond was spiritual rather than earthly, and traces its end — the Latin Church gave it up in the thirteenth century while the Greek Church keeps it still on great occasions such as Easter Day. Robertson observes that in the synagogue men kissed men and women kissed women and that the practice seems never to have been promiscuous between the sexes, which the Apostolical Constitutions independently confirm. Barnes takes the greeting simply of all the Christians with whom Paul was connected at Ephesus.

21.pericope_label: The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand

schools.summary: Gill says the apostle wrote his common salutation in his own hand to prevent counterfeits, so that the church he wrote to might be assured the letter was genuinely his.

Barnes lists what the practice accomplished: it gave a sanction to what was written, proved the letter his own, served as a valuable token of affectionate regard, and was evidence that there was no fraud or imposition — though why Paul employed an amanuensis at all, he says candidly, is not known. Ellicott is willing to name one, holding that the concluding verses are the apostle's autograph while the earlier portions had been written by Sosthenes, whose name stands beside Paul's in the opening greeting. Robertson gives the literal sense as with the hand of me Paul, explains the odd apposition of the genitive with the possessive pronoun, observes that this is the sign in every epistle since Paul dictated but signed at the end, and allows himself a wish most readers will share — if we only had that signature on that scrap of paper.

Clarke would make the grammar show the change of hand, arguing that the clause should be rendered the salutation is written by the hand of me Paul with the verb understood, and thinks it very likely Paul wrote this verse and those following himself while the rest, though dictated by him, was written out by another. Wesley says it in seven words, that what precedes was written by an amanuensis.

22.pericope_label: If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha

schools.summary: Barnes calls this a most solemn and affecting close, aimed at everything the letter has been fighting: the danger was that in their strife over minor matters they should substitute attachment to a party for the love of Christ. He holds the words express a truth about God's dealings rather than any desire of Paul's, and explains why the second phrase mattered — though no earthly power could punish a want of love to Christ, no one could escape, because the Lord would come himself. Ellicott and Robertson both deny the two words belong together: Ellicott would print them as separate sentences and takes the second to mean the Lord is at hand rather than the Lord is come, the uncertainty of the moment being the most solemn thought with which to press the importance of being one with Christ; Robertson calls it a curious blunder in the King James Version that the phrase was ever joined to the curse, reading it instead as a watchword expressing the lively hope of Christ's coming. Robertson agrees that it is the nominal Christian's refusal to love Christ that deserves the word, and Ellicott notes that the term for love signifies not merely affectionate regard but personal devotion.

Calvin identifies the offenders sharply: not strangers who avowedly hated the Christian name, but pretenders and hypocrites who troubled the churches for the sake of their own belly or from empty boasting — and he traces the disorder to its root, since a sincere love to Christ will not suffer us to give occasion of offence to the brethren. He doubts whether Paul seeks their destruction before God or means to render them execrable in the eyes of believers, recalls his reading of a similar curse elsewhere as let him be held by you as accursed, and settles for a plain sense: let them perish and be cut off, as being the pests of the church. On the last word he reports only that almost all the ancients agree the terms are Syriac. Gill rules out one class firmly, that the apostle does not mean profane sinners who lack love to Christ through ignorance, nor even those who from that ignorance persecute him in his members, for such are to be prayed for and are often called by grace afterwards, as he notes the apostle himself was.

Clarke has no doubt the sentence is directed against the Jews, who had called Jesus accursed, and holds that Paul now retorts it upon them; he describes the three Jewish forms — the niddui, a thirty-day exclusion from synagogue, wife and family; the cherem, laid with dire execrations on a man who had not made compensation within those days, though it always left room for repentance; and the shammatha, direst of all, which cut off every hope of reconciliation — yet insists the apostle is not wishing or imprecating but predicting what would certainly come without repentance. Wesley reports the older understanding, that the Jews of that age, having pronounced a man anathema, customarily added the Syriac phrase meaning the Lord cometh, namely to execute vengeance upon him, and adds that Paul chose to write this weighty sentence in his own hand and to set it between the salutation and the benediction so that it might be the more attentively regarded.

23.pericope_label: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you

schools.summary: Gill begins with the formula rather than its content, noting that this is the apostle's salutation in all his epistles and that its presence is itself a token of their truth and genuineness — a signature of authorship and the natural sequel to the verse in which Paul took the pen into his own hand. What it asks has two parts easily run together: first a supply of all grace from Christ, then distinctly the increase of that grace in the saints, a benediction pronounced over people who already possess the thing prayed for. He names four effects of such communications in order — they quicken what was dormant, invigorate what is already alive, draw forth into exercise the grace the saints have received, and enable and assist in the discharge of every duty — so that grace is not only what saves a man at the outset but what continues to move him afterwards.

Clarke's paraphrase widens the single word grace into four, asking that the favour, the influence, the mercy and the salvation procured by Jesus Christ may be with them, and then turns the prayer through three prepositions marking degrees of possession: that this grace may prevail among them, which concerns the church's common life; that it may rule in them, which reaches the individual will; and that it may be exhibited by them, in their life and conversation, which carries it back out into view. Set against the factions and disorders this letter has recorded, the progression reads as a summary of what had been missing.

24.pericope_label: My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen

schools.summary: Ellicott catches the effect of the ending in an image: like a river which, after rushing and foaming over many a rock and through many a gorge, at last emerges into a broad calm amid sunlit meadows, so this epistle, after chapters of trenchant logic and fervid rebuke, closes in peaceful words of tenderness and love. Barnes locates the force of that contrast precisely — the close is peculiarly tender when we remember how many of these people had treated Paul, and that it follows immediately upon the solemn curse of the previous verse — and glosses the last three words as meaning through Christ, or in connection with their own love to him, that is, as Christians. On the note appended after the last verse Barnes is unsparing: it was plainly written by some hand other than Paul's, has no claim whatever to be regarded as inspired, was probably added long after by people not well informed, and is in its main statement false, since the letter itself shows Timothy already away among the churches; none of the manuscript forms carries authority, and because such subscriptions generally mislead the reader it would have been better had they been omitted altogether.

Clarke will not let the sentence stand as it reads, and his objection is a question of sense before it is one of manuscripts. We can easily conceive what the grace of Christ be with you means, since grace is an active, powerful, saving principle without which no individual can be saved; but what could the apostle's love do with them? He confesses he can see no meaning unless it amounts to no more than I love you. He then finds textual support: the possessive pronoun is absent from the Codex Alexandrinus and from an excellent eleventh-century Vatican manuscript, which yields either may love prevail among you or, supplying the word for God as Paul does at the close of the second epistle to this church, the love of God be with you — a sound sense, since the love of God is as much a principle of light and life and salvation as the grace of Christ; and he suspects the pronoun is a copyist's corruption of the divine name. He adds that the closing Amen is wanting in most manuscripts of repute and was certainly not written by the apostle, and calls the subscription palpably absurd, listing the rival forms to show how little any is worth.

Gill offers two ways of taking the words: either the apostle desires to be loved as he loves them, keeping a place in their affections as they had in his, or he commends to them a love of his own reaching all without exception, rich and poor, greater and lesser believers alike — and it is to forestall any suspicion of a merely natural fondness, or one built on outward advantages, that Paul adds the last three words.
